html:
From the 1880s to 1996 the government of Canada, with the churches, ran boarding schools for First Nations, Inuit and Metis children. About 150,000 children were taken, often by force, from their families.

The goal, in the words of the time, was to "kill the Indian in the child". Children were punished for speaking their languages, and many suffered hunger, disease and abuse. Thousands died, and many were buried in unmarked graves. Under the Indian Act attendance became compulsory in 1920.

Survivors' lawsuits led to an apology from Prime Minister Stephen Harper in 2008 and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which in 2015 called the system cultural genocide. Reports of possible graves at Kamloops in 2021 shook the country. The policy grew from the plans of Macdonald's government and ran alongside the potlatch ban.
